title: What Made George Washington So Great? Can it Be Learned?
author: AI Learn Insights
summary: Washington's greatness, the article argues, rested not on brilliance or oratory but on character: self-control, poise, openness to counsel, and practical judgment (Aristotle's phronesis). Historian Joanne Freeman's insight is the article's anchor—people trusted Washington with power because they trusted he would surrender it. His three retirements (1758, 1783, 1797) each modeled the same principle: power is a sacred trust, not a possession, and must be relinquished when the job is done. Washington's models were Cato the Younger (who opposed tyranny) and Cincinnatus (who returned to the farm after saving Rome), and his 'higher education' was entirely practical—surveys, observation, experience. The article ends by posing Washington's final lesson as a question for future exploration: if character produced his greatness, can character be taught?
points: Washington's core advantage was not intelligence or education but character: the ability to govern himself first. His self-control and temper management were deliberate, lifelong practices, not innate gifts, and they made his authority credible in the eyes of those he led.

The three voluntary retirements were not personal modesty but institutional instruction. Each time Washington surrendered power when he could have kept it, he established precedent that power in a republic is a temporary trust from the people, not a lifetime possession of the officeholder.

Openness to counsel was a structural virtue for Washington. He actively sought competing advice, surrounded himself with capable people, despised flattery in all forms, and listened before acting. This was not weakness but a form of epistemic humility that extended his effective intelligence far beyond his formal education.

Practical judgment (phronesis) is what unified Washington's other virtues. It is the capacity to read situations and people, weigh principles against circumstances, and act with flexibility and discernment grounded in experience and moral uprightness. It is the virtue that makes the other virtues politically effective.
quotes: What set him apart then was his character and his sense of justice. The ability to govern himself, to remain steady under pressure, to listen, and to judge well in conditions of uncertainty. That is what made people trust him with power.

Each retirement was an instruction to a fledgling nation. Power is a privilege and a sacred duty. It is also not yours. It is bestowed in trust by the people, and you must give it up when the job is done.
His resignation was extraordinary for its time: a victorious general voluntarily surrendering power.

Washington could governed others because he could govern himself. He was keenly aware of his temper and ambition, and worked throughout his life to keep both in check. His self-control made his authority credible and worthy of trust.

Washington's supreme virtue was good judgment. It's what Aristotle would have recognized as Phronesis, or practical wisdom. It is the capacity to read situations and people, weigh principles against circumstances, and act with flexibility and discernment.
